title: Digital Signals: HIGH and LOW
description: A GPIO pin never says 'sort of'. It only ever says one of two things — and that simple fact is the foundation everything else in this module builds on.

content.value: A Light Switch, Not a Dimmer

Think of a normal light switch on your wall: on or off, nothing in between. A digital GPIO pin works exactly the same way. It's either HIGH (close to the board's operating voltage — 3.3V on the ESP32) or LOW (0V). There's no setting for "a little bit on".

content.title: 📶 Flip the pin
content.hint: Tap the button a few times and watch the trace remember your last taps.

content.value: That trace is a simplified version of a real tool called an oscilloscope, which draws a live graph of a signal's voltage over time. Engineers use one constantly to see exactly this: is a pin actually flipping when the code says it should be?

A GPIO pin set up as an output writes HIGH or LOW — that's how you turn an LED on and off, or tell a motor driver which direction to spin. A GPIO pin set up as an input reads HIGH or LOW — that's how a button press or a simple sensor's signal reaches your program.

OUTPUT PIN                        INPUT PIN
your code decides the voltage     the outside world decides the voltage
"set LED pin HIGH"                "read button pin" → HIGH or LOW
LED lights up                     tells you if it's pressed

Real wires are noisy — tiny fluctuations, interference, a slightly loose connection can all jitter a voltage by a little. If a pin had to distinguish fine shades of voltage, that noise would constantly cause wrong readings. By only asking "closer to 0 or closer to 3.3V?", digital logic becomes extremely reliable even on cheap, imperfect wiring — which is exactly why computers are built on it.
This is also why a computer's memory is measured in bits — a bit is nothing more than one pin's worth of information: a single HIGH or LOW.

Key takeaway: a digital pin only ever reports HIGH or LOW, never in between. That's a deliberate trade — it sacrifices fine detail for reliability, and it's the foundation the whole board is built on.

quiz.question: What are the only two states a digital GPIO pin can report?
quiz.explain: Digital signals are binary by design — close to 0V (LOW) or close to the operating voltage (HIGH), nothing in between.

quiz.question: You want to turn ARIA's status LED on from your program. Is that pin set up as an input or an output?
quiz.explain: Your code is deciding the voltage on that pin (HIGH to light it), which is exactly what an output pin does.

quiz.question: Why do digital pins only report HIGH or LOW instead of a precise voltage reading?
options: It's cheaper to manufacture that way, nothing else
Restricting to two states makes readings reliable even with the small noise and jitter real wires always have
Pins physically cannot measure anything but two values
quiz.explain: Only needing to tell "closer to 0 or closer to full voltage" apart makes the reading robust against the small voltage noise every real circuit has.
